adhd.title: One Step Now: ADHD focus tools to break any task into tiny steps
adhd.meta_desc: A free focus kit for ADHD brains. Type a task and get tiny steps, see only the next one, and make time visible with a visual timer. Works offline, nothing is sent anywhere.
adhd.eyebrow: A focus kit for ADHD brains
adhd.h1_html: Forget the whole mountain. Do one step now.
adhd.lede: Break a task into tiny steps, see only the one in front of you, and make time visible. Everything stays in this browser; nothing is sent anywhere.
adhd.smaller_btn: Too big? Add a smaller step first
adhd.task_ph: e.g. Write a song, or clean my room and call mum
adhd.sugg_note: Made on your device. No AI service, nothing sent.
adhd.sugg_empty: Write what you need to do in the box above, like "clean my room", then press the button.
adhd.own_hint: Or write your own. Make each step small enough that it feels almost silly. "Open the laptop" counts.
adhd.step_ph: Add a tiny step, then press Enter
adhd.no_steps: No steps yet. Add the first tiny one above.
adhd.now_empty: Add a tiny first step below.
adhd.now_alldone: All done. Take a real break.
adhd.times_up: Time's up. Stretch, then choose: keep going or stop.
starters: Set the timer for 2 minutes and promise yourself you can stop when it rings.
Do the step badly on purpose. A messy start beats a perfect plan.
Stand up and walk to where the task happens. That's the whole step.
Say out loud what you're about to do, like you're narrating a cooking show.
Make the first step smaller. Then smaller again.
Text a friend: "I'm starting now." Someone knowing helps.
Put on a song and work only until it ends.
Get a drink of water first, then sit down and open the thing.
Do the most interesting part first. Order is optional.
Work next to someone, in person or on a video call. Having company helps you stay on task.
adhd.cheer_added: Steps added. Just do the first one.
adhd.cheer_skip: Moved to the end. No guilt.
adhd.park_p: A thought pulled at you mid-task? Park it here and get back. You can deal with it later.
adhd.park_empty: Nothing parked. Your head is clear.
adhd.foot_auto: Automatic steps come from built-in rules for common tasks (cleaning, emails, homework, bills, calls, songs, music practice, stories, art and more) and a general method for anything else. They run in your browser with no AI service, so they work offline and cost nothing.
adhd.foot_disclaimer_html: This is a self-help tool, not a diagnosis or treatment. If ADHD is getting in the way of work, school or relationships, a doctor or psychologist can assess you and talk through options. CHADD (chadd.org) has evidence-based information and support groups.
adhd.example_task: Clean the kitchen (example: edit it or start a new task)
example_steps: Put on one song I like
Throw away anything that is rubbish
Wipe the counter next to the sink

ocd.title: Ride the Wave: OCD self-help tools based on ERP
ocd.meta_desc: Free self-help tools for OCD based on exposure and response prevention (ERP): ride out urges, build an exposure ladder and practise living with uncertainty. Private, nothing is sent anywhere.
ocd.eyebrow: Self-help tools for OCD, based on exposure and response prevention (ERP)
ocd.h1_html: The urge rises. You don't have to obey it. Let it pass.
ocd.lede: OCD feeds on rituals and reassurance. Each time you feel the anxiety and don't do the compulsion, your brain learns that you can handle uncertainty. These tools help you practise that. Everything stays in this browser.

cycle.d: A doubt, image or "what if" shows up uninvited.
It feels urgent and dangerous, even when you know it probably isn't.
You check, wash, count, ask for reassurance or go over it in your head.
The anxiety drops for a while, and your brain learns to sound the alarm again.

ocd.cycle_break: ERP breaks the loop at step 3. You let the anxiety be there and skip the compulsion. It's hard at first and gets easier with practice.
ocd.surf_eyebrow: Delay the ritual. Watch the wave.
ocd.surf_p: When an urge to check, wash, count, ask or redo shows up, rate how distressed you feel, then start the timer and hold off on the compulsion. Re-rate every couple of minutes. You'll often see the wave crest and come down on its own. If it doesn't drop today, staying with it still counts.
ocd.suds_label: How distressed do you feel right now? (0 to 10)
ocd.checkin: Two minutes passed. How high is it now? Move the slider and log it.
ocd.started: Started. Hold off on the ritual.
ocd.status_up: It's risen. Waves do that before they fall. Stay with it.
ocd.finished: You stayed with it for {m} min, from {a} to {b}. That's the practice.
ocd.resumed: Picked up where you left off.
ocd.chart_empty: Your ratings will draw a wave here
ocd.example_wave: Example wave shown. Start to draw your own.
prompts: Notice the urge. Name it: "That's OCD." You don't have to argue with it.
Where do you feel it in your body? Describe it like a weather report.
Breathe out slowly. You're not trying to make the feeling go away, just letting it be here.
"Maybe it happened, maybe it didn't. I'm choosing not to find out."
Every minute you wait is practice. This is the work.
The thought feels urgent. Urgency is a feeling, not a fact.
If it's still high, that's okay. Your job is to stay, not to feel calm.
Do something that matters to you while the urge is here. Let it come along.
ocd.ladder_p: List situations that set off your OCD and rate how hard each would be to face without the ritual, from 0 to 100. Start practising around 30 to 50 and move up once a step feels manageable. Repeat each step several times, and lower its number as it gets easier. If you have a therapist, build this ladder with them.
ocd.ladder_ph: e.g. Leave the house after checking the stove once
ocd.rate_hint: Difficulty 0 to 100. The ladder sorts itself from easiest to hardest.
ocd.rate_added: Added. The ladder sorts itself from easiest to hardest.
ocd.ladder_empty: No steps yet. Add a situation above.
ladder_examples: Touch a door handle and wait 10 minutes before washing
Leave the house after checking the stove once
Send an email without re-reading it
Hold the doubt "Did I offend them?" without asking
ocd.unc_p: Instead of answering the doubt, agree that it might be true and carry on. These are tools for the moment the question shows up.

phrases.d: The shortest reply to any doubt. Then carry on.
Certainty isn't on offer. Willingness is.

phrases.t: That's an OCD thought. I don't have to solve it.
phrases.d: Labelling it puts some distance between you and it.

phrases.t: It's possible. I'll live with that.
phrases.d: Agreeing takes the fight out of the doubt.

phrases.t: I can feel anxious and still do this.
phrases.d: Anxiety and action can share the same moment.
Treat the alarm like a smoke detector that goes off when you make toast.
Everyone lives with small risks. You're joining them.

phrases.t: Thoughts aren't facts, and they aren't plans.
phrases.d: Having a scary thought doesn't make it true or mean you want it.

phrases.t: If it matters, I'll find out later. Not now.

ocd.trap_p: Some rituals happen in your head or look like ordinary habits. Open one to see what to try instead.

traps.d: "Are you sure I locked it?" brings relief for a few minutes and makes the next doubt louder. Try: "I notice I want reassurance. I'm going to let the question sit." Let loved ones know they can kindly decline to answer.
Searching for certainty is checking in another form. Close the tab, rate your distress, and ride it out above.
Replaying a conversation or memory to prove nothing bad happened is a ritual. Label it, "I'm reviewing", and bring attention back to what's in front of you.
Avoidance shrinks your life and keeps the fear fresh. Avoided situations are good candidates for your ladder.
Thinking a "good" thought to cancel a "bad" one keeps the cycle going. Let the unwanted thought stay. Thoughts aren't actions, and having one says nothing about who you are.

traps.t: Using this page as a ritual
traps.d: If you notice yourself logging or re-reading here to feel certain, that's a compulsion too. Close the page and get on with your day.

ocd.help_p1_html: These tools support treatment; they don't replace it. ERP with a trained therapist, and sometimes medication, help most people with OCD feel much better. The International OCD Foundation directory (iocdf.org) lists therapists who specialise in OCD.
ocd.help_p2_html: If you are in crisis or thinking about harming yourself, call your local emergency number or a crisis line now. Find A Helpline (findahelpline.com) lists free crisis lines by country.
ocd.contact_note: This form isn't a crisis or support service, and it's read by one person, not a therapist. Please don't include private health details. If you are in crisis, call your local emergency number.
